title: A Day on Venus Is Longer Than a Year!
description:
If you lived on Venus, your birthday would come before tomorrow does. How? Gizmo the robot finds out! 🚀
A how-things-work Short for curious kids ages 4–8 from Gizmo Explains.

Venus spins very, very slowly. One spin takes 243 Earth days! But one trip around the Sun only takes 225 days. So a day on Venus is longer than its whole year! And Venus spins backward, too.

title: Planets for Kids! 5 Space Surprises with Gizmo
description:
Join Gizmo the robot for a 5-minute space adventure! Visit Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, and learn a surprise fact about each one. 🚀
Made for curious kids ages 4–8: guess-the-planet clues, move-along fun, and a recap at the end.

What we learn today:
• A year on Mercury is only 88 days.
• Venus spins backward.
• Mars is red because of rust.
• Jupiter is the biggest planet.
• And Saturn could float in a giant bathtub!

title: Jupiter Has a Storm Bigger Than Earth!
description:
You've seen rain storms. Jupiter has one storm bigger than the whole Earth! Where is it? Gizmo the robot finds out! 🚀
A how-things-work Short for curious kids ages 4–8 from Gizmo Explains.

It's called the Great Red Spot. Can you see it? This storm is so big, the whole Earth could fit inside it! Jupiter is the biggest planet, and it's made mostly of gas. There's no ground to stand on!

title: Saturn Could Float in a Bathtub!
description:
Your rubber duck floats in the bath. Saturn could float too, in a giant bathtub! Why? Gizmo the robot finds out! 🚀
A how-things-work Short for curious kids ages 4–8 from Gizmo Explains.

Saturn is huge, but it's very light for its size. It's made mostly of gas. So in a giant, giant bathtub, Saturn would float! And its beautiful rings are made of chunks of ice and rock.

title: Moon Footprints Can Last Millions of Years!
description:
Your footprints in the sand wash away. On the Moon, footprints can stay for millions of years! Why? Gizmo the robot finds out! 🚀
A how-things-work Short for curious kids ages 4–8 from Gizmo Explains.

The Moon has no wind and no rain. So nothing comes along to wipe the footprints away! Astronauts walked on the Moon more than fifty years ago, and their footprints are still there.
